discovery.note: Cavendish made it by dropping metals into acid and showed it burns to form water; Lavoisier named it in 1783.

nameOrigin: Greek hydro (water) + genes (forming): it makes water when it burns.

radioactive.note: Tritium, used in glowing exit signs and fusion research.

elementalForm.description: Two hydrogen atoms each share their single electron, making one shared pair: a single covalent bond. With that pair both atoms have the helium-like full first shell.

allotropes.name: Orthohydrogen and parahydrogen
allotropes.note: Two forms of H2 that differ only in whether the two nuclear spins are parallel or opposite.

bulk.note: Solid hydrogen is a crystal of H2 molecules.

originNote: Almost all hydrogen formed in the first minutes and hundreds of thousands of years after the Big Bang.
appearance: Colorless, odorless gas; glows pink-violet in an electric discharge.
summary: Hydrogen is the simplest and most common element: one proton and one electron. It makes up about three-quarters of the ordinary matter in the universe and powers the stars by fusing into helium.
uses: Fuel cells and rocket fuel (liquid hydrogen)
facts: About 74% of the ordinary mass in the universe is hydrogen.
A hydrogen atom without its electron is just a proton.
Every water molecule contains two hydrogen atoms.
biology: Essential: part of water, all organic molecules and DNA; about 10% of human body mass.
hazards: Extremely flammable; mixtures with air from 4% to 75% hydrogen can explode.

discovery.note: Seen as an unknown yellow line in the Sun's spectrum during an eclipse; found on Earth by William Ramsay in 1895.

nameOrigin: Greek helios, the Sun, where it was first detected.

elementalForm.description: Helium's two electrons completely fill its only shell, so its atoms have no reason to share or exchange electrons. It forms no stable chemical compounds and exists as single atoms.

bulk.structure: Hexagonal close-packed (only under pressure above 25 atm)
bulk.note: At normal pressure helium stays liquid down to absolute zero.

originNote: Most helium was made in the Big Bang; stars add more by fusing hydrogen.
appearance: Colorless gas; glows orange-pink in a discharge tube.
summary: Helium is the second lightest and second most abundant element in the universe. It is so unreactive and so weakly attracted to itself that it never freezes at normal pressure.
uses: Cooling superconducting magnets in MRI scanners
Lifting gas for balloons and airships
facts: Liquid helium below 2.17 K becomes a superfluid that can creep up the walls of its container.
Almost all helium on Earth comes from radioactive alpha decay in rocks and is collected from natural gas.
hazards: Not toxic, but breathing pure helium displaces oxygen and can cause suffocation.

discovery.note: Found in the mineral petalite; first isolated as a metal by electrolysis in 1855.

nameOrigin: Greek lithos, stone, because it was found in a mineral.

elementalForm.description: Each lithium atom gives its one outer 2s electron to a shared sea of electrons. The positive Li+ cores are held together by that negative sea: metallic bonding.

originNote: A little lithium came from the Big Bang; more came from cosmic rays splitting heavier nuclei and from some aging stars.
appearance: Soft, silvery-white metal that tarnishes quickly in air.
summary: Lithium is the lightest metal and the least dense solid element: it floats on water (while reacting with it). It is the key ingredient in rechargeable batteries.
uses: Lithium carbonate as a mood-stabilizing medicine
facts: Lithium is so light it would float on oil.
It burns with a crimson-red flame.
biology: No essential role known; lithium salts treat bipolar disorder.
hazards: Reacts with water to release flammable hydrogen; causes burns.

discovery.note: Found as an oxide in beryl and emerald; the metal was isolated in 1828 by Wöhler and Bussy.

nameOrigin: From beryl, the mineral it was found in.

radioactive.note: Made by cosmic rays in the air; used to date ice and sediments.

elementalForm.description: Beryllium atoms pool their two 2s electrons in a shared electron sea. Its bonding has more directional, covalent character than most metals, which makes it stiff and brittle.

originNote: Almost all beryllium was made when cosmic rays smashed into carbon, nitrogen and oxygen nuclei in space.
summary: Beryllium is a very light but extremely stiff metal. It is nearly transparent to X-rays, which makes it valuable for windows in X-ray tubes and detectors.
uses: Mirrors of the James Webb Space Telescope (gold-coated beryllium)
Copper-beryllium spring alloys and non-sparking tools
facts: Emerald and aquamarine are both varieties of the beryllium mineral beryl.
Beryllium is about six times stiffer than steel for its weight.
hazards: Inhaled beryllium dust can cause chronic beryllium disease, a serious lung illness.

discovery.by: Joseph Louis Gay-Lussac; Louis Jacques Thénard; Humphry Davy
discovery.note: Isolated impure from boric acid; pure boron was only made in 1909.

nameOrigin: From borax, the mineral it was extracted from (Arabic buraq).

elementalForm.description: Boron has only three valence electrons, too few for ordinary pairs everywhere. Its atoms form B12 icosahedra held together by multi-center bonds, where one electron pair is shared by three atoms.

allotropes.name: Beta-rhombohedral boron
allotropes.note: The most stable form, built from linked B12 icosahedra.

allotropes.name: Alpha-rhombohedral boron
allotropes.note: A simpler packing of single icosahedra.

bulk.note: A very complex structure; the viewer shows one B12 icosahedron.

originNote: Like lithium and beryllium, boron was made mostly when cosmic rays split larger nuclei.
appearance: Black-brown lustrous crystals or brown powder; extremely hard.
summary: Boron is a metalloid with too few electrons to bond in ordinary ways, so it builds icosahedral clusters. Boron compounds make heat-proof glass, hard abrasives and detergents.
uses: Boron fibers and boron carbide armor
Control rods in nuclear reactors (boron-10 absorbs neutrons)
facts: Boron carbide is one of the hardest known materials.
Boron-10 captures neutrons so well it is used in cancer therapy.
biology: Essential for plants (cell walls); trace amounts may help human bone health.
hazards: Elemental boron is of low toxicity; some boron compounds such as boranes are highly toxic.

discovery.note: Charcoal and soot have been used since prehistory; Lavoisier showed diamond is carbon in 1772.

radioactive.note: Made by cosmic rays in the air; used for radiocarbon dating.

elementalForm.description: In graphite each carbon shares electron pairs with three neighbors in flat hexagonal sheets, and its fourth electron is delocalized across the sheet, so graphite conducts electricity. In diamond each carbon shares a pair with four neighbors in a rigid 3D network.

allotropes.name: Graphite
allotropes.note: Stacked sheets of hexagons; soft, black and conductive.

allotropes.name: Diamond
allotropes.note: A 3D tetrahedral network; the hardest natural material.

allotropes.name: Graphene
allotropes.note: A single sheet of graphite one atom thick.

bulk.note: Carbon sublimes at about 3,915 K at normal pressure instead of melting.

originNote: Made by fusing three helium nuclei in stars, then spread by aging stars and supernovae.
appearance: Black, soft graphite or clear, very hard diamond.
summary: Carbon can share electrons with up to four partners, including other carbon atoms, so it forms chains, rings and networks. That makes it the backbone of millions of compounds and of all known life.
uses: Fuels: coal, oil and natural gas are carbon compounds
Diamonds for cutting tools and jewelry
Graphite in pencils, batteries and lubricants
facts: More compounds contain carbon than any other element except hydrogen.
Diamond and graphite are the same element, just bonded differently.
biology: The basis of all organic molecules; about 18% of human body mass.
hazards: Carbon itself is of low toxicity; fine soot and dust harm the lungs.

discovery.note: Found as the part of air that would not support burning or life after carbon dioxide was removed.

elementalForm.description: Each nitrogen atom shares three of its five outer electrons, giving three shared pairs: a triple bond. Each atom keeps one lone pair. The triple bond is one of the strongest bonds known, which makes N2 very unreactive.

originNote: Made by the carbon-nitrogen-oxygen fusion cycle in stars.
appearance: Colorless, odorless gas; a clear liquid below 77 K.
summary: Nitrogen makes up 78% of the air. Its triple bond is hard to break, so living things depend on special bacteria, lightning and the Haber process to turn it into usable compounds.
uses: Inert atmosphere for food packaging and electronics
Liquid nitrogen for freezing and cryogenics
facts: About 78% of each breath you take is nitrogen.
Liquid nitrogen boils at −196 °C.
biology: Essential: in every amino acid, protein and DNA base.
hazards: Not toxic, but can displace oxygen and suffocate; liquid nitrogen causes frostbite.

discovery.note: Scheele made it around 1771–72 but published late; Priestley published in 1774.

nameOrigin: Greek oxys (sharp, acid) + genes (forming): Lavoisier wrongly thought all acids contain it.

elementalForm.description: Two oxygen atoms share two electron pairs, a double bond, and each keeps two lone pairs. The full picture is subtler: O2 has two unpaired electrons, which makes liquid oxygen magnetic.

allotropes.name: Ozone (O3)
allotropes.note: A bent three-atom molecule that shields Earth from ultraviolet light.

originNote: Made by helium fusion inside massive stars and scattered by their supernovae.
appearance: Colorless gas; pale blue as a liquid and solid.
summary: Oxygen is the most abundant element in Earth's crust and the third most abundant in the universe. It pulls electrons strongly, so it combines with almost every element and drives burning and breathing.
facts: Liquid oxygen is attracted to magnets.
Almost half of the mass of Earth's crust is oxygen, mostly locked in rocks.
biology: Essential: used by cells to release energy; about 65% of human body mass.
hazards: Pure oxygen makes fires burn far more fiercely.

discovery.note: Isolated by electrolysis after decades of attempts that injured or killed several chemists; Moissan won the 1906 Nobel Prize.

nameOrigin: From the mineral fluorite (Latin fluere, to flow), used as a flux.

radioactive.note: Used in FDG for PET cancer scans.

elementalForm.description: Two fluorine atoms share one electron pair, a single bond, and each keeps three lone pairs. The bond is weak because the lone pairs crowd each other, which is one reason fluorine is so reactive.

originNote: Made in small amounts in massive stars and some aging stars; fluorine is easily destroyed in stellar cores.
appearance: Pale yellow gas; yellow liquid below 85 K.
summary: Fluorine is the most electronegative element: it pulls electrons harder than any other. It reacts with nearly everything, even glass and some noble gases.
uses: Fluoride in toothpaste and drinking water
facts: Fluorine can react with xenon, a 'noble' gas.
Water, glass and steel wool can burn in a stream of fluorine.
biology: Fluoride strengthens tooth enamel; not known to be essential.
hazards: Extremely toxic and corrosive gas; reacts violently with most substances.

discovery.note: Found by distilling liquefied air; its bright red glow was the first clue.

elementalForm.description: Neon's second shell is full (8 electrons), so its atoms neither share nor exchange electrons. No stable neutral neon compound is known.

bulk.note: Atoms held only by weak van der Waals forces.

originNote: Made by carbon fusion in massive stars.
appearance: Colorless gas; glows red-orange in a discharge tube.
summary: Neon is a noble gas famous for the red-orange glow of neon signs. It is the least reactive of all elements.
facts: Only the red-orange signs actually contain neon; other colors use other gases or coatings.
Neon is the fifth most abundant element in the universe but rare on Earth.
hazards: Harmless except as a suffocation risk in enclosed spaces.

discovery.note: Isolated by passing electricity through molten sodium hydroxide.

nameOrigin: From soda; the symbol Na is from Latin natrium.

radioactive.note: A positron emitter used in research.
Used as a medical and industrial tracer.

elementalForm.description: Each sodium atom releases its single 3s electron into a shared electron sea that binds the Na+ cores. With only one electron per atom the bonding is weak, so sodium is soft and melts at 98 °C.

originNote: Made by carbon fusion in massive stars.
appearance: Soft, silvery metal, easily cut with a knife; tarnishes at once in air.
summary: Sodium is a soft, very reactive metal. It gives up its outer electron so readily that it is never found free in nature, but its ion Na+ is everywhere, from sea salt to nerve signals.
uses: Table salt and many sodium compounds
facts: Sodium reacts with water so vigorously that the hydrogen released can catch fire.
Sodium gives fireworks and street lamps their yellow-orange color.
biology: Essential: Na+ carries nerve impulses and controls body fluid balance.
hazards: Reacts violently with water; causes burns.

discovery.note: Black recognized magnesia as a new element's oxide; Davy isolated the metal by electrolysis in 1808.

nameOrigin: From Magnesia, a district in Greece known for magnesium minerals.

elementalForm.description: Magnesium atoms each release two 3s electrons into a shared electron sea around Mg2+ cores.

originNote: Made by carbon and neon fusion in massive stars.
summary: Magnesium is a light, strong metal that burns with a dazzling white flame. It sits at the heart of every chlorophyll molecule.
uses: Lightweight alloys for cars, aircraft and laptops
Antacids and laxatives (magnesium hydroxide and sulfate)
facts: Burning magnesium cannot be put out with water: it keeps burning and releases hydrogen.
Each chlorophyll molecule holds one magnesium ion at its center.
biology: Essential: needed by hundreds of enzymes and by ATP; central to chlorophyll.
hazards: Powder or ribbon is flammable; burning magnesium is very hard to extinguish.

discovery.note: Ørsted made impure aluminium in 1825; Friedrich Wöhler made purer metal in 1827.

nameOrigin: From alum (Latin alumen), a salt of aluminium.

radioactive.note: Made by cosmic rays; its gamma rays are seen across the Milky Way.

elementalForm.description: Each aluminium atom contributes three valence electrons to the shared electron sea that binds the Al3+ cores.

originNote: Made by carbon and neon burning in massive stars.
summary: Aluminium is the most abundant metal in Earth's crust. It is light and resists corrosion because a thin oxide skin seals its surface.
facts: In the 1850s aluminium was more precious than gold; the tip of the Washington Monument is aluminium.
Recycling aluminium saves about 95% of the energy needed to make it from ore.
hazards: Low toxicity; fine powder is flammable.

discovery.note: Made by heating potassium fluorosilicate with potassium.

elementalForm.description: Like carbon in diamond, each silicon atom shares one electron pair with each of four neighbors, building a 3D tetrahedral network.

originNote: Made by oxygen fusion in massive stars and in white-dwarf explosions.
appearance: Hard, brittle, blue-grey crystals with a metallic shine.
summary: Silicon is a semiconductor and the second most abundant element in the crust, mostly as silica and silicates. Purified silicon crystals are the foundation of computer chips and solar cells.
facts: Sand is mostly silicon dioxide.
Chip-grade silicon is purified to better than 99.9999999%.
biology: Used by diatoms and some plants to build skeletons; trace role in humans uncertain.
hazards: Low toxicity; breathing crystalline silica dust causes silicosis.

discovery.note: Brand boiled down large amounts of urine while searching for the philosopher's stone and got a glowing substance.

nameOrigin: Greek phosphoros, light-bearer, because white phosphorus glows in air.

radioactive.note: Used in biology research and medicine.

elementalForm.description: White phosphorus is made of P4 tetrahedra: each atom shares one pair with each of the other three and keeps one lone pair. The 60° bond angles are strained, which makes white phosphorus very reactive.

allotropes.name: White phosphorus (P4)
allotropes.note: Waxy, glows in air and ignites by itself near 30 °C.

allotropes.name: Red phosphorus
allotropes.note: Chains of linked P4 units; used on match boxes.

allotropes.name: Black phosphorus
allotropes.note: Layered like graphite; the most stable form.

originNote: Made by neon and oxygen burning in massive stars.
appearance: White phosphorus is a waxy, pale solid; red phosphorus is a dark red powder.
summary: Phosphorus is essential to life: it forms the backbone of DNA and the energy carrier ATP. Its pure forms range from dangerously reactive white phosphorus to stable red and black phosphorus.
facts: Phosphorus was the first element discovered by a known person.
Your bones and teeth are mostly calcium phosphate.
biology: Essential: DNA, RNA, ATP, cell membranes and bones.
hazards: White phosphorus is very toxic and ignites spontaneously in air.

discovery.note: Known since ancient times as brimstone; Lavoisier recognized it as an element in 1777.

nameOrigin: Latin sulfur (or sulphur), the ancient name.

radioactive.note: Made by cosmic rays; a tracer in biology.

elementalForm.description: Sulfur atoms form crown-shaped rings of eight. Each atom shares one pair with each of its two neighbors in the ring and keeps two lone pairs.

allotropes.name: Rhombic sulfur (alpha-S8)
allotropes.note: The stable yellow crystals at room temperature.

allotropes.name: Plastic sulfur
allotropes.note: Rubbery long chains made by pouring hot sulfur into water.

originNote: Made by oxygen fusion in massive stars and in white-dwarf explosions.
summary: Sulfur is a yellow nonmetal found near volcanoes. Its compounds give rotten eggs and skunks their smell, and sulfuric acid is the world's most-produced industrial chemical.
facts: Jupiter's moon Io is coated in sulfur from its volcanoes.
Molten sulfur turns blood red and thick as it is heated.
biology: Essential: in the amino acids cysteine and methionine and in many vitamins.
hazards: Elemental sulfur has low toxicity; burning it forms toxic sulfur dioxide.

discovery.note: Scheele made it but thought it contained oxygen; Humphry Davy showed it was an element in 1810.

elementalForm.description: Two chlorine atoms share one electron pair (a single bond); each keeps three lone pairs, completing an octet of eight electrons.

originNote: Made by oxygen burning in massive stars.
summary: Chlorine is a reactive halogen that grabs one electron to become the chloride ion in table salt. It kills microbes, which made chlorinated drinking water one of the great public-health advances.
facts: Your stomach makes hydrochloric acid to digest food.
Chlorine was used as a weapon in World War I.
biology: Essential as chloride ion: stomach acid and body-fluid balance.
hazards: Toxic, corrosive gas that damages the lungs.

discovery.note: Found because nitrogen taken from air was slightly heavier than nitrogen made from chemicals.

radioactive.note: Used to date groundwater and ice.

elementalForm.description: Argon's outer shell holds a full octet, so its atoms stay single. Only one neutral argon compound, HArF, has been made, and only below −246 °C.

originNote: Argon-36 and -38 come from stars; the argon-40 in our air comes from radioactive potassium-40 decaying in rocks.
appearance: Colorless gas; glows lilac in a discharge tube.
summary: Argon is the third most common gas in air (about 0.93%). Being inert, it protects hot metals and filaments from oxygen.
facts: Almost all of Earth's argon came from radioactive potassium.
There is more argon in a room than carbon dioxide.
hazards: Can displace oxygen in enclosed spaces.
